result: The authors generated a new Ube3a knockout mouse model (Ube3aΔe6) by deleting exon 6, which results in diminished Ube3a mRNA and protein (2-17% of WT) in the brain. This new model shows similar behavioral phenotypes to the previously established Ube3aΔe5 model but has more complete transcript knockdown.
evaluation: Claims C40-C45 provide converging evidence from RT-ddPCR (C43), Western blots (C44), and behavioral assays (C45) that the new Ube3aΔe6 allele is a valid Angelman syndrome model. The molecular characterization is thorough with appropriate controls comparing to the existing Ube3aΔe5 model.

result: Both Ube3a-as ASO and Snord115 ASO decrease Ube3a-ATS transcripts and increase Ube3a mRNA levels in WT mice. In Ube3am+/pYFP mice, these ASOs reactivate paternal Ube3a-YFP expression to 40-90% (Ube3a-as) and 20-60% (Snord115) of maternal expression levels across multiple brain regions including GABAergic neurons.
evaluation: Claims C46-C50 are supported by RT-ddPCR data (C46-C47) and immunofluorescence imaging (C48-C49) showing dose-dependent reactivation of the paternal allele. The spatial distribution across brain regions and cell types is well-documented in Figure 2.

result: ASO treatment of juvenile Ube3amΔe6/p+ mice increases Ube3a protein to 28-71% of WT levels at 3 weeks post-injection, with corresponding decreases in Ube3a-ATS (29-73%) and increases in Ube3a mRNA (22-57%). Ube3a-as ASO effects remain stable for 10 weeks, while Snord115 ASO effects diminish by 6 weeks. Both Ube3a isoforms 2 and 3 are similarly upregulated.
evaluation: Claims C51-C57 are supported by comprehensive Western blot and RT-qPCR data across multiple brain regions and timepoints (Figures 3-4). The differential durability between the two ASOs is clearly demonstrated, and the critical isoform 3 upregulation is confirmed.

result: In Ube3amΔe6/p+ mice, Ube3a-ATS levels negatively correlate with both Ube3a protein and mRNA levels, while Ube3a protein levels positively correlate with Ube3a mRNA levels across different brain regions and timepoints.
evaluation: Claims C58-C60 are supported by correlation analyses in Figure 4C and supplements showing strong relationships (R² values 0.35-0.91) across multiple brain regions. The correlations are mechanistically consistent with the antisense repression model.

result: Control ASO-treated Ube3amΔe6/p+ mice show increased EEG power in 8-25 Hz and decreased power in 50-100 Hz compared to WT mice. Ube3a-as ASO treatment normalizes these abnormalities in juvenile mice, reducing the power ratio (α+β1+β2)/γ2 to WT levels. Snord115 ASO shows similar effects at 3 weeks but diminishes over time.
evaluation: Claims C61-C68 are supported by comprehensive EEG power spectral density analyses (Figure 5) with appropriate statistical comparisons. The normalization of the power ratio provides a robust quantitative measure of phenotypic rescue that tracks with ASO efficacy.

result: Ube3amΔe6/p+ mice show selective reduction in REM sleep during the light phase, recapitulating Angelman syndrome patient phenotypes. ASO treatment in juvenile mice normalizes REM sleep at 3 and 6 weeks post-injection, with both Ube3a-as and Snord115 ASOs showing efficacy.
evaluation: Claims C69-C71 are supported by automated sleep scoring data (Figure 6) validated against expert manual scoring. The selective REM sleep deficit and its rescue by ASO treatment are clearly demonstrated with appropriate statistical analyses.

result: Control ASO-treated Ube3amΔe6/p+ mice show significantly more poly-spikes in frontal and somatosensory cortices but not visual cortex compared to WT mice. Neither Ube3a-as nor Snord115 ASO treatment significantly reduces poly-spike frequency in juvenile or adult mice, although Snord115 ASO shows a non-significant 50% reduction.
evaluation: Claims C72-C75 are supported by systematic poly-spike quantification (Figure 7) showing region-specific hyperexcitability that is not rescued by ASO treatment. The lack of rescue is clearly demonstrated despite successful Ube3a upregulation, indicating this phenotype requires different intervention.

result: EEG relative power in theta, alpha, and beta bands negatively correlates with Ube3a protein levels, while gamma band power positively correlates. The power ratio (α+β1+β2)/γ2 negatively correlates with Ube3a levels. REM sleep time during light phase positively correlates with Ube3a levels. Delta band power shows no correlation.
evaluation: Claims C76-C81 are supported by comprehensive correlation analyses (Figure 8) combining data across ASO types, injection ages, and timepoints. The strong correlations (R² 0.56-0.91 for most measures) demonstrate dose-dependent relationships between Ube3a levels and phenotypic outcomes.

result: A single ICV injection of Ube3a-ATS-targeted ASOs upregulates Ube3a proteins including the critical isoform 3 and restores EEG power spectrum and sleep patterns for at least 6 weeks, with greater efficacy when administered at juvenile versus adult age.
evaluation: Claims C82-C83 summarize the main findings supported by the comprehensive molecular, electrophysiological, and behavioral data presented throughout the results. The age-dependent efficacy is clearly demonstrated by comparing juvenile and adult treatment cohorts.

result: Poly-spikes are mechanistically independent from EEG power spectrum and sleep pattern deficits in Ube3amΔe6/p+ mice.
evaluation: Claim C84 is supported by the differential response to ASO treatment: EEG power spectrum and sleep are rescued (C63-C68, C71) while poly-spikes are not (C74-C75), despite similar Ube3a upregulation. This dissociation indicates distinct underlying mechanisms.

result: The improvement in EEG power spectrum and sleep pattern tracks with Ube3a protein levels across different ASOs, injection ages, and timepoints, suggesting these phenotypes are acutely modulated by Ube3a levels that decrease over time due to ASO clearance.
evaluation: Claims C85-C86 are supported by the strong correlations shown in Figure 8 and the temporal dynamics of both Ube3a levels (Figure 3) and phenotypic measures (Figures 5-6). The parallel time courses provide compelling evidence for acute dose-dependent modulation.

result: ASO treatment in adult mice is less effective than in juvenile mice for rescuing EEG and sleep phenotypes.
evaluation: Claim C87 is supported by direct comparison of juvenile versus adult treatment cohorts showing reduced Ube3a upregulation (Figure 3F) and diminished phenotypic rescue (Figures 5F-I, 6D-F) in adult-treated mice. This is consistent with cited literature (Spencer et al., 2022).

result: A power ratio between low- and high-frequency EEG bands is proposed as a more robust measure of EEG power spectrum phenotype in Angelman syndrome than absolute power in individual frequency bands.
evaluation: Claim C88 is supported by the consistent elevation of (α+β1+β2)/γ2 ratio across timepoints (C65) and its strong correlation with Ube3a levels (C78), compared to variable results for individual bands in prior literature. The ratio accounts for concurrent changes in multiple frequency bands.

result: The therapeutic window for genetic therapies in Angelman syndrome is broader than previously thought based on prior work showing rescue only in early development. EEG power spectrum and sleep architecture are recommended as outcome measures for evaluating therapy efficacy.
evaluation: Claims C11-C12 are supported by the successful rescue of EEG and sleep phenotypes in juvenile and adult mice (C63-C68, C71), contrasting with prior literature showing limited rescue of other phenotypes at these ages (C5-C6, C28, C31-C32). The recommendation is justified by the robust, quantifiable, and dose-dependent responses of these measures.

result: Background claims establish that UBE3A encodes ubiquitin ligase E3A, is paternally imprinted in neurons via UBE3A-ATS antisense transcript, and maternal deficiency causes Angelman syndrome characterized by multiple neurological symptoms including abnormal EEG and sleep disturbance.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C13-C21 represent well-established background knowledge supported by multiple citations to foundational literature. These provide the scientific rationale for the therapeutic approach tested in this study.

result: Prior work in Angelman syndrome mouse models demonstrates multiple robust phenotypes including motor, behavioral, EEG, sleep, and synaptic deficits. Most phenotypes can only be rescued by reinstating Ube3a in early development, and ASO/AAV therapies show limited efficacy when administered postnatally. Three clinical trials with ASOs are currently underway.
evaluation: Claims C22-C35 summarize prior literature establishing the rationale and context for the current study. These are appropriately cited and provide the motivation for testing ASO efficacy at juvenile and adult ages for EEG and sleep phenotypes not previously examined.

result: Alterations in EEG power spectrum (particularly increased 1-30 Hz power) and sleep disturbance are well-documented in both Angelman syndrome patients and mouse models. Delta band power correlates with symptom severity in patients.
evaluation: Claims C36-C39 establish the clinical relevance of the EEG and sleep phenotypes examined in this study, supported by multiple citations. These justify the focus on these specific outcome measures.

result: Reactivating paternal UBE3A by suppressing UBE3A-ATS is a promising therapeutic approach, but prior work suggests the therapeutic window may be restricted to early development.
evaluation: Claims C4 and C6 establish the therapeutic rationale and the key question addressed by this study. These are supported by the cited literature on rescue experiments (C5, C28, C31-C32) showing age-dependent efficacy.

result: About 70% of Angelman syndrome patients have larger deletions in 15q11-q13 encompassing UBE3A and other genes. Deletion patients show more severe phenotypes and larger EEG abnormalities than non-deletion patients, suggesting heterozygosity of biallelically expressed genes contributes to disease severity.
evaluation: Claims C89-C92 are supported by cited clinical literature and provide important context for interpreting the translational relevance of the mouse model results. The inference about gene dosage effects (C92) is reasonable but requires future experimental validation.

result: EEG power spectrum can serve as a quantitative biomarker in clinical trials based on its correlation with Ube3a levels in this study and with symptom severity in patients. ASO treatment may improve cognitive function in patients, though this is speculative.
evaluation: Claim C93 is supported by the strong correlations in this study (C76-C78) and cited patient literature (C37, C94). However, C95 is explicitly speculative and lacks direct evidence. The biomarker utility requires validation in clinical trials.

result: Sleep disturbance is considered one of the most challenging symptoms by clinicians and caregivers. If ASO therapy reduces sleep disturbance, it will improve quality of life for patients and caregivers.
evaluation: Claim C96 is supported by citation to patient/caregiver survey data. Claim C97 is a logical inference contingent on successful translation of the mouse findings to patients. The conditional statement is appropriately qualified.

result: Abnormal EEG rhythms and sleep disturbance are prominent clinical features of Angelman syndrome, and the degree of phenotypic improvement in mice correlates with Ube3a protein levels.
evaluation: Claim C9 is established clinical knowledge supported by citations. Claim C10 is a key finding supported by the correlation analyses in Figure 8 (C76-C81). These claims connect the clinical relevance to the mechanistic findings.
